newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan steps up verbal intervention on currency.
newsitem.headline: Japan steps up verbal intervention on currency.

text.p: Japan on Thursday stepped up its effort to prop up the faltering yen with verbal threats to intervene on currency markets.

Comments by finance officials sent the dollar, which hit a more than four-and-a-half year high of 127 yen in New York on Wednesday, below 126 yen for a bit and the U.S. unit was hovering just above 126 yen in late Tokyo trade.
But some currency strategists said they were still sceptical over whether Japan would back words with action.

Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka, in a speech to bank executives, said the yen's recent fall against the dollar had been excessive and that Japan would deal "decisively" with any such excessive moves.

Adding to a prepared speech, Mitsuzuka said: "We will act decisively in a timely manner when exchange rates move excessively. The recent movement of the yen is obviously excessive, and I am concerned about it."
Close on the heels of Mitsuzuka's comments were remarks by senior Finance Ministry official Eisuke Sakakibara, known as "Mr Yen" for his influence in currency markets.

Sakakibara told Reuters that intervention in foreign exchange markets by Japanese authorities was possible if exchange rates deviated greatly from economic fundamentals and said movements in the dollar/yen rate were not in line with such fundamentals.
"We do not think (dollar/yen movements) are in line with economic fundamentals. (The movements) are clearly too rapid," Sakakibara said.
Sakakibara, director-general of the Finance Ministry's international finance bureau, also said Japan was in close touch with U.S. officials on foreign exchange matters.
The dollar fell to just below 126 yen from around 126.50 yen on fears that the Bank of Japan (BOJ) might finally be poised to intervene to buy yen.
Reading from the same script, Vice Finance Minister Tadashi Ogawa echoed the comments in a news conference later.
But dealers said there was no sign of action by the central bank, and some strategists said they doubt whether Japan is ready yet to put its money where its mouth is.

"I don't think it really indicates a shift in policies -- it's reminiscent of the talk in January and February (when the yen also fell sharply against the dollar)," said Kenneth Landon, senior currency strategist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.

"I'm sceptical whether the BOJ is willing to take decisive action. The main reason is that I don't think the U.S. Treasury at this point would be very keen. The U.S. Treasury market is very fragile and any hint of concerted intervention would be taken very poorly in the U.S. treasury market," he added.

The dollar's rise against the yen has been largely fuelled by the gap between higher U.S. interest rates, which many expect to rise further, and rock-bottom rates in Japan. Many economists expect Tokyo to keep its hyper-easy credit policy at least until autumn because of banking sector woes.

Japanese finance mandarins, concerned about a flare-up in trade friction with Washington as Japan's trade surplus grows, have begun repeating their mantra that sharp shifts in exchange rates -- either up or down -- are undesirable.
But some trade officials have admitted that for now, the benefits of a weak yen for Japan's economy outweigh the disadvantages.
